reasoning: Patient is alert and responsive—rules out ESI 1 (no immediate life-saving intervention required).
Chief complaint is isolated traumatic laceration to knee; no reported loss of consciousness, head injury, or polytrauma.

Vitals NOT RECORDED: This is a critical gap. Pediatric patients require age-specific vital assessment. At age 6, normal HR ~70–110, RR ~20–25, BP ~95–105 systolic. Without recorded vitals, cannot definitively rule out high-risk physiology (shock, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension).
Healthy baseline, up-to-date immunizations, no medications/allergies, and alert mental status reduce concern for occult systemic illness or sepsis.
Injury mechanism (fall on playground) is low-mechanism, isolated laceration 3 cm over knee—does NOT mandate imaging or advanced intervention at triage.

Expected resource utilization: wound exploration/irrigation, possible suturing (procedural sedation may be needed in a 6-year-old), and dressing—at minimum two resources (exam + procedure ± anesthesia/medication).
ESI-3 typically requires ≥2 resources with stable physiology. ESI-4 would apply if only wound care/bandaging planned without imaging/labs/sutures.

SAFETY CONCERN: Absence of vitals in a pediatric trauma patient introduces uncertainty. Triage must obtain vitals immediately to exclude compensated shock (especially relevant post-trauma). However, clinical appearance (alert, cooperative, no severe distress noted) and mechanism suggest stability.
No red flags for head trauma, compartment syndrome, vascular injury, or systemic infection based on history alone; however, thorough exam needed.
red_flags: VITALS NOT RECORDED—mandatory in any pediatric patient, especially post-trauma; obtain immediately before final assignment.
First-time patient with no prior record; no collateral history from caregivers on mechanism severity, loss of consciousness, or other injuries.
Pediatric trauma warrants vigilance for occult head injury or multi-system involvement despite apparent focal injury.
If vitals are abnormal (tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension) or altered mental status develops, escalate to ESI 2.
